findings.location: design.md#Decision: Birth dates live on the profile
findings.recommendation: Define retention by purpose, not by profile lifetime: when a member opts out, clear `birthday` and `phone` at once (add a requirement and scenario for withdrawing the opt-in — the spec has none); state how long nightly backups keep them and that restores re-apply opt-outs and deletions; make access, rectification, erasure and portability exports cover the two new columns (GDPR Art. 5(1)(c)(e), Art. 17, Art. 20). Failing scenario: a member opts out, yet their birthday and mobile number stay in `profiles` and in every backup for as long as the account exists, with no purpose left.
findings.title: Birthday and phone kept after opt-out and in backups with no expiry

findings.location: design.md#Decision: Greetings are sent by SMS through Textly
findings.recommendation: Send Textly only the phone number and a message text that carries no identifier beyond what the greeting needs; the spec only requires "a text message", not a named one (data minimisation, Art. 5(1)(c)). Failing scenario: every birthday, each member's display name is posted alongside their phone number to a US processor, which then holds a name-to-number mapping it never needed.
findings.title: Display name sent to Textly though the greeting does not need it

findings.location: design.md#Decision: Greetings are sent by SMS through Textly
findings.recommendation: Question for the team: the transfer outside the EEA is identified, but the plan names no Chapter V safeguard (adequacy under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, or SCCs), no Art. 28 processor agreement, and no limit on how long Textly keeps the phone numbers and message logs — so erasure on our side would miss Textly's copies. Record what was decided in design.md.
findings.title: US transfer to Textly with no stated safeguard, processor terms or retention

findings.evidence: Members enjoy being remembered; marketing wants birthday messages.
findings.recommendation: Question for the team: state the purpose and lawful basis (presumably consent, given the opt-in, Art. 6(1)(a)) and whether the texts count as direct marketing under the ePrivacy Directive; if so, the opt-in wording and an easy way to withdraw (e.g. STOP reply or profile toggle) belong in the spec. Only the controller can decide this.
findings.title: Lawful basis for marketing birthday texts not stated
